title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 62 (Further Issue of Share Capital)

content.overview: Section 62 governs further issue of share capital: a pro-rata rights offer to existing equity holders is the default, with statutory routes for ESOPs, preferential issues and certain conversion terms.
content.glance: Section 62 governs further issue of share capital: a pro-rata rights offer to existing equity holders is the default, with statutory routes for ESOPs, preferential issues and certain conversion terms.
content.study: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 62 (Further issue of share capital). When a company with share capital proposes to increase subscribed capital by issuing further shares, the default under section 62(1)(a) is an offer to existing equity shareholders in proportion, as nearly as circumstances admit, to paid-up share capital on their shares. The letter of offer must state the number offered and the statutory acceptance period (ordinarily 15–30 days); unless the articles provide otherwise, the offer includes a right of renunciation. After rejection or expiry, the Board may dispose of the shares in a manner not disadvantageous to shareholders and the company. Alternative routes include an ESOP under section 62(1)(b), subject to special resolution, and an issue to any persons under section 62(1)(c), subject to special resolution and prescribed conditions including valuation. Check any private-company rule permitting a shorter rights-offer period only where its exact consent conditions are met. Section 62 also addresses conversion of loans/debentures into shares where the terms were approved by special resolution before issue, and Government-directed conversion in the circumstances stated in subsections (4)–(6). Section 42 private placement and section 23 issue modes may also apply depending on the transaction. This topic remains under rule-level and case-law review.

sections.heading: Rights issue — default route
sections.body: Further shares are offered to existing equity holders pro rata to paid-up capital as nearly as circumstances admit. The letter of offer states the number offered and the statutory acceptance period, ordinarily 15–30 days. Unless the articles otherwise provide, the offer includes a right of renunciation.

sections.heading: Disposition of declined/unaccepted shares
sections.body: After the offer is declined or expires, the Board may dispose of the shares in a manner not disadvantageous to the shareholders and the company. Apply the statutory condition to the actual allotment.

sections.heading: Employee stock option route
sections.body: Further shares may be offered to employees under an employees' stock option scheme authorised by special resolution, subject to applicable rules.

sections.heading: Preferential issue
sections.body: Further shares may be offered to any persons, whether or not including existing shareholders or employees, if authorised by special resolution and the prescribed conditions are met, including valuation where required. Private-placement requirements may also apply.

sections.heading: Conversion and Government-directed issue
sections.body: Section 62 includes separate provisions for conversion of loans/debentures into shares where the terms were approved by special resolution before issue, and for Government-directed conversion in the circumstances and subject to the procedure in subsections (4)–(6).

sections.heading: Private-company shorter period and connected routes
sections.body: Do not assume the ordinary rights-offer period can be shortened automatically. Check the current private-company rule and its exact consent conditions. Distinguish section 62 further issue from section 42 private placement and the issue modes in section 23.

examples.title: Rights offer
examples.body: The company sends a letter of offer to equity holders pro rata, with a 21-day acceptance window and renunciation right. Section 62 rights route is followed.

examples.title: Preferential issue
examples.body: By special resolution and with prescribed valuation, the company issues further shares to a strategic investor. Section 62 preferential route is used.

hypotheticals.question: A company wants to allot further shares to a strategic investor rather than first offering them pro rata to existing equity holders. What route must be analysed?
hypotheticals.analysis: The default is a rights offer under section 62(1)(a). An issue to other persons requires the special-resolution and prescribed conditions under section 62(1)(c), including valuation where required; section 42 private-placement requirements may also apply.

hypotheticals.question: A company wants to use a shorter rights-offer period in a private company. Can it simply set a shorter deadline?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Verify the current private-company rule and satisfy its exact written/electronic consent conditions before using a shorter period.

distinctions.title: Further issue and private placement
distinctions.left: Section 62 governs rights, ESOP and preferential further-issue routes.
distinctions.right: Section 42 governs the separate private-placement procedure where applicable.

rows.left: Shareholder pre-emption and permitted further-issue routes
rows.right: Offer/invitation to identified persons and private-placement compliance

misconceptions.trap: Assuming the Board can always issue further shares to any person without shareholder approval.
misconceptions.correction: The default is a pro-rata rights offer; ESOP and preferential routes require the relevant special resolution and prescribed conditions.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming renunciation is always excluded or always unconditional.
misconceptions.correction: Unless the articles otherwise provide, the rights offer includes renunciation; apply the articles and applicable rules.

misconceptions.trap: Treating section 62 preferential issue and section 42 private placement as interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the separate requirements of each provision where the transaction engages them.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined a share issue and allegations of oppression.
cases.issue: Whether the share issue was legally valid and oppressive.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The validity and fairness of a share issue are assessed by reference to statutory power, purpose and the facts; dilution alone does not establish oppression.
cases.holding: The Court assessed the share issue within the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Relevant context for share-issue purpose and oppression, not a substitute for section 62's text.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the default route for further issue of shares?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: A pro-rata offer to existing equity shareholders under section 62(1)(a), subject to the statutory period, renunciation and disposal provisions.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Does a preferential issue require only a Board decision?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: No. Section 62(1)(c) requires a special resolution and prescribed conditions, including valuation where required.

Check whether section 42 private placement and section 23 also apply.
